title: The Grande Rue to the Panthéon: the Battle of Hernani, Nineteen Years at Sea, and the Poor Man's Hearse
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Child Carried After the Army

stops.name: Besançon, birth on the Grande Rue
stops.date_confidence: attested; day and street given in the civil record and in every biography
stops.campa: In a house on the Grande Rue a third son is born to Joseph-Léopold-Sigisbert Hugo, an officer climbing through Bonaparte's army, and Sophie Trébuchet, a Breton whose loyalties run the other way, toward the old kings. The marriage is a quarrel with two people inside it, and the child takes both halves: he will be a royalist at twenty and a republican at fifty and will spend a lifetime arguing that the change was growth. They name him Victor-Marie, after the officer who introduced his parents. The garrison moves on within the year and the family with it.
suggested_refs: The birth house on the Grande Rue, Besançon, preserved as a small museum

stops.name: Avellino, the father's province
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: the chronology sources date the journey 1807, one biographical account 1808; the family is in Avellino across both years and the month is not fixed
stops.campa: Sophie Hugo brings her three sons over the Alps to join their father, who serves the province under Joseph Bonaparte in a hill town inland from Naples. Victor is five. What he keeps of Italy is fragmentary and permanent: roads held by brigands, a countryside pacified by an occupying army his own father helps command. He hears a language spoken before he can place it. The reunion does not repair the marriage. Sophie takes the boys back to Paris; their father stays in Italy with the army, and from this year the parents live in separate countries.
suggested_refs: The former convent at Avellino used as the French governor's residence

stops.name: Paris, the garden of the Feuillantines
stops.date_confidence: the tenancy runs roughly 1809 to 1813; no month fixed in the sources, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Sophie installs her sons in a former convent on the rue des Feuillantines, where the garden has run wild for years. There are three boys, a ruined chapel, fruit trees nobody prunes, and a priest hired to teach them Latin. Hugo will write this garden for sixty years, in the Odes and in Les Contemplations: the fixed point of the childhood, the last place before the separations begin in earnest. He is seven when it starts and eleven when it ends. Nothing after it, not the Place Royale and not Hauteville House, gets described in his verse with the same undefended warmth.
suggested_refs: The site of the convent garden on the rue des Feuillantines, built over in the nineteenth century
sources: Hugo, 'Ce siècle avait deux ans' and the Feuillantines poems

stops.name: Fuenterrabía, crossing into Spain
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1811 by Adèle Hugo's Victor Hugo raconté (1863) and Robb; the exact day is not recorded
stops.campa: Nine years old, in a convoy of vehicles moving under armed escort, Victor crosses the Bidasoa into a country at war with the army escorting him. His father now serves King Joseph in Madrid and has sent for the family. The road runs for weeks past burned villages and bodies left at the verge by both sides; the convoy travels closed up and the guerrilla is never more than a hill away. He is not yet a writer and takes no notes. Forty years later the executions he saw on that road are still coming back to him in print.
suggested_refs: Adèle Hugo, Victor Hugo raconté par un témoin de sa vie (1863), on the Spanish convoy

stops.name: Madrid, the Real Colegio de San Antonio Abad
stops.date_confidence: attendance attested; the month of entry is not fixed in the sources and the building's exact site is approximate
stops.campa: Victor and his brother Eugène are entered as boarders among the sons of Spanish nobility, in a seminary school where the French children of the occupation are given a corner and a wide berth. He learns Latin, some Spanish, and the particular cold of being on the winning side and unwelcome for it. His father is a general of the intruder king; the families of his classmates are in the field against that king. Within the year the war turns, the boys are taken back to Paris, and the marriage ends in a legal separation.
suggested_refs: The Real Colegio de San Antonio Abad, Madrid, school of the French officers' sons under Joseph Bonaparte

stops.name: Lycée Louis-le-Grand, the boarder who writes verse
stops.date_confidence: the schooling runs 1815 to 1818; no month fixed in the sources, defaulted to January
stops.campa: His father, having won custody, lodges him at the Pension Cordier and sends him up to Louis-le-Grand for the mathematics and the law a candidate for the Polytechnique needs. Hugo attends and fills his notebooks with verse instead. At fifteen the Académie française gives an honourable mention to a poem he has entered in its annual competition, and the judges, taking the author for a grown man, want his age confirmed before they will print it. He supplies it. He does not sit the Polytechnique examination, and the law course is left unfinished.
suggested_refs: The Académie française concours of 1817 and its record of the mention honorable

stops.name: Église Saint-Sulpice, the marriage to Adèle Foucher
stops.date_confidence: attested by the parish and civil records; the gap from his mother's death is fifteen months, not the two years given in one account
stops.campa: He marries the girl he has known since the Feuillantines garden, fifteen months after his mother's death removed the last objection to it. The first book of Odes has appeared, Louis XVIII has granted a pension on the strength of it, and at twenty the marriage is affordable. His brother Eugène, in love with Adèle himself and silent about it for years, breaks down during the wedding celebrations and is committed. He will spend the rest of his life in an asylum. Hugo signs the register with his brother already gone from the room.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of Saint-Sulpice, 12 October 1822

stops.name: Bibliothèque de l'Arsenal, the Cénacle at Nodier's table
stops.date_confidence: the Cénacle evenings run roughly 1824 to 1827; no single date applies
stops.campa: Charles Nodier, librarian of the Arsenal, keeps an apartment inside the library and an open evening in it, and the young men who mean to break the rules of French verse gather there: Sainte-Beuve, Vigny, Dumas, painters, critics, anyone with a grievance against the unities. Hugo arrives as one of them and leaves as their head. In 1827 he publishes Cromwell, a play too long to stage, with a preface demanding that the grotesque be admitted beside the sublime and that the classical rules be abolished outright. The preface is read everywhere. The play is not performed.
suggested_refs: The Préface de Cromwell (1827), founding manifesto of French Romanticism

stops.name: Comédie-Française, the battle of Hernani
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinates here are the Salle Richelieu, place Colette, correcting a pin that fell 290 m north in the Palais-Royal
stops.campa: Hugo refuses the paid claque and packs the pit with his own party instead: art students, poets, Théophile Gautier in a waistcoat visible from every seat in the house. The classicists come to hiss a first line that runs its sense across the break of the verse, and they hiss it. The play runs for weeks against organised interruption, both camps arriving early to hold their ground, the fighting continuing in the newspapers by day. The pit does not settle the merits of the tragedy. It settles who holds the French stage. He is twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: Théophile Gautier's Histoire du romantisme, written as a participant in the pit

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Paris, the word in the tower
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the March publication month is not carried by the verified sources, so the date defaults to January
stops.campa: He has been climbing the towers for years, in a cathedral the Revolution stripped and the city is letting rot, and he writes the book to save the stone. The novel is set in 1482 and its real subject is what the nineteenth century is doing to what the fifteenth built. Work on the fabric begins again within twenty years. In the preface he reports finding a Greek word cut by hand into a dark corner of a tower, fate, and being unable to find it again afterward. Nobody else records seeing it. He is the only witness the inscription ever had.
stops.quote: A few years ago, while visiting or, rather, rummaging about Notre-Dame, the author of this book found, in an obscure nook of one of the towers, the following word, engraved by hand upon the wall:
stops.quote_source: Notre-Dame de Paris, Preface, tr. Isabel F. Hapgood (Project Gutenberg ebook 2610). The word that follows is printed there in Greek as ἈΝÁΓΚΗ (ananke, fate); the forms ANANKH and ANANKE appear nowhere in that text.
suggested_refs: Luc-Olivier Merson's illustrated edition of Notre-Dame de Paris
The Viollet-le-Duc and Lassus restoration of Notre-Dame, begun 1844

segments.name: Place Royale: the Peer of France

stops.name: 6 Place des Vosges, the second floor on the Place Royale
stops.date_confidence: the tenancy runs 1832 to 1848; no month fixed in the sources
stops.campa: The family takes the second floor of the Hôtel de Rohan-Guéménée on the Place Royale, rooms around a square of red brick built for Henri IV, and stays sixteen years. Here he writes the plays, the poetry of the July Monarchy, and the first abandoned draft of the novel that will become Les Misérables; here he receives the political and literary traffic of a decade. Adèle keeps the salon, and by the middle of the decade the marriage is a household arrangement and nothing warmer. Paul Meurice gives the apartment to the city in 1902 and it opens to the public the following June.
suggested_refs: The Maison de Victor Hugo, 6 place des Vosges, opened to the public 30 June 1903 after Paul Meurice's 1902 donation
sources: Maison de Victor Hugo, Paris Musées

stops.name: Paris, the night of the sixteenth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the couple kept the date as their anniversary for fifty years
stops.campa: Juliette Drouet plays a small part in Lucrèce Borgia, and on the night of the sixteenth Hugo goes to her. She is twenty-six and has been kept by other men; she leaves the stage, her debts follow her for decades, and she spends the next fifty years copying his manuscripts in a hand he prefers to his own. She writes him something close to twenty thousand letters. He keeps the marriage, the household, the other liaisons and her, all at once, and she keeps the anniversary of this night every year until she dies.
suggested_refs: The Juliette Drouet correspondence, some twenty thousand surviving letters

stops.name: Paris, Andersen at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Andersen's own record of his 1833 Paris stay
stops.campa: A Danish writer of twenty-eight, three months into his first long journey south and a day from leaving the city, calls on Hugo and is received. Hans Christian Andersen has already sought out Heine in Paris that summer; he is collecting the living the way other travellers collect cathedrals. Hugo is thirty-one, author of Notre-Dame de Paris and winner of the fight at the Comédie-Française, and gives him a signature and an afternoon. Neither man has yet written the book he will be remembered for. Andersen's first fairy tales appear in two years.
suggested_refs: Andersen's 1833 Paris diary, dating the call on Hugo to 14 August

stops.name: Institut de France, elected on the fourth candidacy
stops.date_confidence: election date attested; the pin is the Institut de France, quai de Conti, correcting a coordinate that fell 400 m south near Saint-Germain-des-Prés
stops.campa: The Académie française has refused him three times, on the grounds that he is the head of a party rather than a man of letters. On the fourth attempt, in January, it yields, and the leader of the Romantics takes a seat among the guardians of the rules his Cromwell preface set out to abolish. His opponents say in advance that he will use the chair as a platform and that a platform is not what the chair is for. He is received under the cupola in June. The peerage follows four years after that.
suggested_refs: The reception speech under the coupole, Institut de France, June 1841

stops.name: Cirque de Gavarnie, the Pyrenees before the news
stops.date_confidence: the Pyrenean journey is dated to August 1843; the day at Gavarnie is not recorded
stops.campa: He is travelling with Juliette Drouet through the Pyrenees and the Basque country, a summer of walking and notebooks, and stands in front of the limestone wall at the head of the valley: an amphitheatre with waterfalls falling the whole height of it. He writes it down as architecture, a cathedral nobody built. His daughter has been married since February and he is in no hurry home. The travel notes from this summer are published long after his death, and he never in his life reads them straight through.
suggested_refs: Hugo's Pyrénées, the 1843 travel notes published posthumously

stops.name: Villequier, the boat on the Seine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates set to the village centre, the sources carrying three pins spread across two kilometres
stops.campa: Léopoldine Hugo, nineteen, married six and a half months, goes out on the Seine below Villequier in a small boat with her husband and two of his family. A squall takes the boat over on a wide reach of tidal river. Charles Vacquerie, a strong swimmer, dives repeatedly for his wife and drowns with her. Hugo is on the road north with Juliette Drouet and learns of it days later from a newspaper somebody has left on a café table. The two are buried in the churchyard here. He writes nothing for months. Then he writes Les Contemplations.
suggested_refs: The Vacquerie tomb in the churchyard of Villequier
Hugo, 'À Villequier' and 'Demain, dès l'aube', Les Contemplations

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, peer of France
stops.date_confidence: peerage ordinance attested to the day; the pin corrects a coordinate that had been set on the Panthéon, 230 m south
stops.campa: Louis-Philippe raises him to the peerage and he takes his seat in the upper chamber, a poet with a legislature. He speaks for Poland, against the death penalty, on misery as a thing a government can be asked to abolish. In July of the same year the police find him in a rented room with Léonie Biard, the wife of a painter. A peer of France cannot be taken on a commissary's word, so he walks out of the room and goes back to the chamber. She is arrested for adultery and held at Saint-Lazare.
suggested_refs: The Saint-Lazare prison register for Léonie d'Aunet, July 1845

segments.name: The Republic, and the Second of December

stops.name: Paris, elected to the Constituent Assembly
stops.date_confidence: corrected: he was not elected in the general vote of 23 April 1848 but on 4 June, in the complementary elections for the Seine
stops.campa: He is elected six weeks after the general vote, in the complementary elections for the Seine, and takes his seat as a conservative in a republic he had not asked for. The June insurrection breaks out within weeks and is put down by the army at a cost of thousands of lives. Hugo votes that summer with the party of order and then spends three years walking away from it, speech by speech: against the death penalty, against the deportation of political prisoners, for free compulsory schooling, for misery treated as a legislative object rather than a fact of nature.
suggested_refs: Hugo's Assembly speeches of 1848 to 1851, collected as Actes et paroles: Avant l'exil

stops.name: Paris, the opening of the Peace Congress
stops.date_confidence: date of the congress attested; the English wording of the address is quoted from Wikiquote and has not been checked against the French original
stops.campa: He presides over an international peace congress meeting in Paris, with English and American delegates in the hall, and opens it by proposing that the nations of the continent will one day be fused into a higher unity without losing their names or their distinctness: a United States of Europe, with a senate where there are now armies. The hall applauds. The address goes out with the printed proceedings of the congress, in English and in French, to governments none of which act on it. Two years and four months later he leaves France on a false passport.
stops.quote: A day will come when there will be no battlefields, but markets opening to commerce and minds opening to ideas.
stops.quote_source: Opening address to the Peace Congress, Paris, 21 August 1849, as quoted on Wikiquote; translation and exact wording unverified against the French text
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the 1849 Paris Peace Congress

stops.name: Paris, the campaign for the captive emir
stops.date_confidence: no date fixed in the sources; the captivity at Amboise runs 1848 to 1852 and the press campaign belongs somewhere inside it
stops.campa: Abdelkader, who fought the French army in Algeria for seventeen years and surrendered on written terms of passage to Alexandria, is instead shut up with his household in the château of Amboise on the Loire, where twenty-five of his people sicken and die. France has broken its word and knows it. Hugo and Émile de Girardin take the case up in print, arguing the promise as a debt owed by the nation rather than a favour to be granted a prisoner. The emir is released in 1852 by the same man who by then has driven Hugo out of the country.
suggested_refs: The Paris press campaign for Abdelkader's release, 1848 to 1852
sources: Château d'Amboise, notes on the emir's captivity

stops.name: Paris, the second of December
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the flight follows on 11 December
stops.campa: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte dissolves the Assembly by night, arrests the deputies likely to resist, and takes the state. Hugo does not go home. For four days he moves between rented rooms and printers with a handful of republican representatives, drafting appeals to arms that are posted on walls and torn down within the hour, standing on an omnibus on the boulevards to call the troops back to the Republic. The barricades are thin and the army fires into the crowds. On the eleventh he crosses into Belgium on a false passport in a workman's name.
suggested_refs: Hugo, Histoire d'un crime, written 1877 from the notes of December 1851

stops.name: Brussels, a room on the Grand-Place
stops.date_confidence: arrival date attested; the room on the Grand-Place is documented in Hugo's own account
stops.campa: He arrives with almost nothing and takes a room overlooking the Grand-Place, in a city already filling with proscribed Frenchmen. Adèle and his daughter follow; his sons are in prison in Paris and come later. He writes standing, at speed, and in seven months finishes a hundred-page indictment of the man who has taken France. The Belgian government, nervous of its large neighbour, sends word that the pamphlet cannot be printed on Belgian soil and that its author would do well to be somewhere else on the day it appears.
suggested_refs: Hugo, Choses vues, on the first weeks of the Brussels exile

stops.name: Brussels and London, Napoléon le Petit
stops.date_confidence: corrected: published simultaneously at Brussels and London on 8 August 1852, not written or published on Jersey, where Hugo had arrived only three days earlier
stops.campa: The pamphlet comes out in Brussels and London on the same day, three days after its author has crossed to Jersey. It is banned in France and gets in anyway, in editions small enough to hide, and it sells in the tens of thousands. Napoleon III has been named the Little by the greatest living French writer and cannot get the name off. The Empire answers by seizing what Hugo still owns in France and by asking every government he lives under to move him along. Belgium complies, and Jersey complies. Guernsey does not.
suggested_refs: Hugo, Napoléon le Petit (Brussels and London, 8 August 1852)

stops.name: Marine Terrace, the house on the Grève d'Azette
stops.date_confidence: occupied 16 August 1852 to 31 October 1855; coordinates corrected to the Grève d'Azette in the parish of Saint-Clément, roughly two kilometres southeast of a pin previously set in Saint-Hélier town
stops.campa: The house he rents from a Jersey shipowner stands on the Grève d'Azette outside the town, with nothing between it and the sea but the road. He lives in it three years and describes it as a whitewashed thing with the look of a tomb. The Channel is grey most of the year, and on clear days the coast of France is a line on the horizon, near enough to make the exile a daily fact rather than a position. Here he begins Les Contemplations, and here he writes ninety-eight poems against one man and calls them Les Châtiments.
suggested_refs: Marine Terrace, Grève d'Azette, Saint-Clément, Jersey, demolished 1974

stops.name: Marine Terrace, the tables that speak
stops.date_confidence: the séances begin in the autumn of 1853 and run about two years; the verified sources carry only the year
stops.campa: A visitor from Paris teaches the household the turning table, and for two years the exiles sit at it in the evenings. The table answers, and the names it gives are Shakespeare, Dante, Molière, Luther, the Ocean, Death, and Léopoldine. Hugo has hundreds of sessions transcribed in verse and prose and publishes not a line of them while he lives, warned that the notebooks would be read as proof of madness. That the sessions happened is on paper in his own household's hand. What was speaking at the table is not a question paper can settle.
suggested_refs: The Jersey séance transcripts, published only in the twentieth century as Les Tables tournantes de Jersey

stops.name: Saint Helier, the expulsion
stops.date_confidence: corrected: he left Jersey on 31 October 1855, not in September; and he was expelled for refusing a declaration of allegiance, not simply for signing the offending letter
stops.campa: A newspaper of the French exiles, L'Homme, prints a letter attacking Queen Victoria over her state visit to Napoleon III. Three of its men are expelled from the island; Hugo signs a protest, and is told he may stay if he will sign a declaration of allegiance in return. The demand comes from the island's own authorities and not from Paris. He refuses to sign it. On the last day of October he crosses to Guernsey, after three years and two months on Jersey, and Belgium had moved him on before that.
suggested_refs: The L'Homme letter of 1855 and the Jersey expulsion order

stops.name: Hauteville House, bought with a book of grief
stops.date_confidence: purchase 16 May 1856, moved in 5 November 1856; coordinates corrected by roughly 550 m to 38 rue de Hauteville
stops.campa: Les Contemplations appears in April in two volumes, Autrefois and Aujourd'hui, divided by the date of his daughter's drowning, and it sells out. With the money he buys a house above Saint Peter Port outright and in his own name, which makes him a property owner under the British crown and much harder to expel. He moves in on the fifth of November. He spends the next fourteen years decorating it himself, cutting mottoes into the panelling and building whole rooms out of chests and altar fronts bought off the island's dealers.
suggested_refs: Hauteville House, 38 rue de Hauteville, given to the City of Paris by Hugo's descendants in 1927

stops.name: Hauteville House, the look-out and the refusal
stops.date_confidence: corrected from [R] to attested: this is a dated public declaration of 18 August 1859, not a traditional attribution
stops.campa: At the top of the house he builds a room of glass, open to the light on every side, and writes there standing at a shelf, facing south across the water toward a coast visible on clear days. In August the Emperor proclaims a general amnesty for the proscribed and most of the exiles go home. Hugo publishes his answer in the newspapers. He is fifty-seven and has already been eight years out of France; the sentence he prints commits him to eleven more, and to the books that would not have been written in Paris.
stops.quote: Quand la liberté rentrera, je rentrerai.
stops.quote_source: Public declaration on the imperial amnesty, 18 August 1859 (fr.wikipedia, 'Exil de Victor Hugo')
suggested_refs: The glass look-out at the top of Hauteville House, preserved as he left it

stops.name: Mont-Saint-Jean, walking the field of Waterloo
stops.date_confidence: the battlefield visit is dated to May 1861; no day recorded
stops.campa: He comes to Belgium in May to write a battle into the middle of a novel about a convict and a bishop, and walks the ground for weeks: the sunken road of Ohain, the wall at Hougoumont, the slope the cuirassiers went up. He sketches the terrain and takes lodgings on the field itself. The chapters he is writing will stop the novel dead for fifty pages, and he knows it, and writes them anyway, because the century he is describing turns on this field and he was thirteen years old when it turned.
suggested_refs: Hugo's Waterloo notebooks, Bibliothèque nationale de France
sources: Hugo, Les Misérables, Part II Book I

stops.name: Hôtel des Colonnes, Mont-Saint-Jean, the last line
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the manuscript dateline is 30 June 1861, not 30 May; and the inn stood at Mont-Saint-Jean, not at Genappe seven kilometres south
stops.campa: He finishes Les Misérables in a room at an inn beside the battlefield and dates the manuscript from it, one of the few times in his life he completes a book anywhere but at his own desk. Seventeen years earlier the first version was abandoned when his daughter drowned; since then the manuscript has followed him through a coup, three countries and two islands. He writes to his son that the book is done and that he can die now. He is fifty-nine and has twenty-four years left.
suggested_refs: The manuscript dateline of Les Misérables, Hôtel des Colonnes, 30 June 1861
sources: standard editions of Les Misérables, editorial apparatus

stops.name: Hauteville House, the letter to Captain Butler
stops.date_confidence: the verified sources carry only the year 1861 for the letter, so the date defaults to January
stops.campa: An English officer writes from China asking the most famous writer in Europe to approve, for the record, the burning of the Summer Palace at Yuanmingyuan by the Anglo-French expedition. Hugo answers from the island and refuses in terms the officer cannot have wanted. He describes a wonder built by a whole people over generations, and two European armies going through it like burglars sharing out a museum, and he names them. The letter is not published in France in his lifetime. He signs it from the house on Guernsey.
stops.quote: Two robbers breaking into a museum. One has looted, the other has burnt. ... one of the two conquerors filled its pockets, seeing that, the other filled its safes; and they came back to Europe laughing hand-in-hand. ... Before history, one of the bandits will be called France and the other England.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Captain Butler, 'Expédition de Chine' (1861), as quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Old Summer Palace'; translator unnamed there and the passage is given with ellipses, so the joins are compressed rather than verified word for word
suggested_refs: The ruins of the Yuanmingyuan, Beijing, where the letter is displayed at the site

stops.name: Brussels, Les Misérables published
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the staggered 1862 publication months are not carried by the verified sources
stops.campa: Lacroix brings out the first part in Brussels and Paris and the rest across the year, and the queues form before the shops open. It is translated and pirated within months and is a bestseller on two continents before the French critics have finished being cold about it. He is sixty, and forty years out from the first Odes. The preface is dated from the island and states the case for the book as a public utility rather than a work of art: as long as there is ignorance and poverty on the earth, books like this one cannot be useless.
stops.quote: So long as there shall exist, by virtue of law and custom, decrees of damnation pronounced by society, artificially creating hells amid the civilization of earth, and adding the element of human fate to divine destiny; so long as the three great problems of the century, the degradation of man through pauperism, the corruption of woman through hunger, the crippling of children through lack of light, are unsolved; so long as social asphyxia is possible in any part of the world; in other words, and with a still wider significance, so long as ignorance and poverty exist on earth, books of the nature of Les Miserables cannot fail to be of use.
stops.quote_source: Les Misérables, Author's Preface, signed Hauteville House, 1862 (English Wikisource); em dashes in that text replaced with semicolons, no words altered
suggested_refs: The Lacroix first edition of Les Misérables, Brussels and Paris, 1862

stops.name: Guernsey, Les Travailleurs de la mer
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month carried by the verified sources
stops.campa: He writes a novel about a Guernsey fisherman who goes out alone to take the engine out of a wrecked ship, against the rock and the tide and the octopus, and who gives up everything he wins by it at the end. He dedicates the book to the island that sheltered him. The local dialect word pieuvre, for octopus, enters standard French out of this novel and stays there. Visitors begin arriving on Guernsey to look at a rock in the sea because a proscribed Frenchman wrote a book about it in a glass room above the harbour.
suggested_refs: Hugo's dedication of Les Travailleurs de la mer to the island of Guernsey

stops.name: Brussels, the death of Adèle Hugo
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the verified sources; the August day is not carried by them
stops.campa: Adèle Hugo, married to him forty-six years, dies in Brussels, where the family gathers each summer because Guernsey was never a place she could love. He is with her at the end. He arranges her burial at Villequier beside their daughter and follows the coffin as far as the French frontier, where he stops, still proscribed and unwilling to enter France on the Emperor's terms even for this. The rest of the family goes on without him. He turns back toward the island and the desk.
suggested_refs: The Hugo family graves in the churchyard at Villequier

segments.name: The Return, and the Year of Deaths

stops.name: Gare du Nord, nineteen years later
stops.date_confidence: attested; the verified chronology carries the month, the geography lens the day
stops.campa: Sedan falls on the second, the Empire on the fourth, and on the evening of the fifth Hugo's train comes into the Gare du Nord after nineteen years. He is sixty-eight and has outlived the regime that proscribed him by a week. Fifteen years remain to him, and he will spend all of them in France. The crowd is on the platform and in the street outside and will not disperse; they half carry him away, and he speaks to them from a carriage, telling them to save Paris and to save the Republic.
suggested_refs: Hugo's Actes et paroles: Depuis l'exil, opening with the return of September 1870

stops.name: Paris, the ramparts through the siege
stops.date_confidence: the siege runs from September 1870 to January 1871; no single date applies and the pin is a general position on the eastern ramparts
stops.campa: He stays through four months of Prussian siege and refuses every offer of a way out. The receipts of a benefit performance of his own work are given to cast cannon for the walls, and the guns are named after him and after his books. The city eats its horses, then its cats, then the animals of the zoo, and Hugo, who is sent dinners by admirers, writes down what has been served him: elephant, bear, antelope, on the menus of restaurants still pretending to have menus. He is shelled, he is hungry, and he keeps the diary.
suggested_refs: Hugo, Choses vues, and the Paris press of the 1870-71 siege
sources: contemporary Paris press accounts of the siege

stops.name: Bordeaux, the Assembly and the death of Charles
stops.date_confidence: Charles Hugo's death attested to the day; the February election that brought Hugo to Bordeaux is carried as reconstruction in the verified sources
stops.campa: The National Assembly meets at Bordeaux to ratify the peace, and Hugo sits in it for three weeks, speaks against the cession of Alsace and Lorraine, is shouted down over Garibaldi, and resigns. Five days later his son Charles, forty-four, dies of apoplexy in a cab on his way to dinner. Hugo has now buried a daughter, a wife and a son. He takes the coffin north by train and buries it at Père-Lachaise on the eighteenth of March, the day the Commune rises, the National Guard in the street stopping to salute a hearse they take for one of their own.
suggested_refs: The Hugo family vault at Père-Lachaise, where Charles Hugo was buried 18 March 1871

stops.name: Place des Barricades, Brussels, the stones through the window
stops.date_confidence: May 1871, no day fixed; address corrected from a hotel that belonged to another writer's biography entirely
stops.campa: After the Commune is put down he publishes an offer from Brussels: his house is open to any defeated Communard Belgium refuses asylum to, and the police may come for him there instead. A crowd comes first, at night, fifty or sixty men throwing paving stones through his windows while his grandchildren are asleep in the house. The Belgian government expels him within days, for the offence of having offered shelter. He goes to Vianden in Luxembourg and stays the summer.
suggested_refs: 4 place des Barricades, Brussels, attacked in May 1871
The Maison Victor Hugo at Vianden, Luxembourg

stops.name: Paris, the last of the sons
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: François-Victor Hugo dies of tuberculosis at forty-five, having spent the years of the exile translating the complete Shakespeare into French, eighteen volumes begun on Jersey and finished on Guernsey. Of five children born to the marriage, one is now left: Adèle, brought home unwell from the Caribbean the year before, who will outlive her father by decades in a house at Saint-Mandé. Hugo is seventy-one and has outlived four of the five. The following year he publishes Quatre-vingt-treize, set in the Terror in the Vendée, and never writes another novel.
suggested_refs: François-Victor Hugo's complete French Shakespeare, begun on Jersey
Hugo, Quatre-vingt-treize (1874)

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, the senator of the Third Republic
stops.date_confidence: election date attested; pin corrected from the Panthéon to the Palais du Luxembourg
stops.campa: Elected senator for Paris at seventy-three, he walks back into the chamber he first entered thirty-one years earlier as Louis-Philippe's peer and sits at the far left of it. His first speech asks a full amnesty for the Communards, and he asks again, session after session, before a Republic that does not want to hear it. The chamber hears him out with every mark of respect and votes the other way. He is by now unbeatable at the polls. The amnesty passes in 1880, four years after he first moved it.
suggested_refs: Hugo's Senate speeches for the Communard amnesty, 1876 to 1880

segments.name: The Avenue That Takes His Name

stops.name: Avenue d'Eylau, the parade and the new name
stops.date_confidence: two events, often conflated and both misdated to an eightieth birthday that fell on 26 February 1882: the parade beneath his window was 27 February 1881, the renaming of the avenue 28 June 1881
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of February 1881, entering his eightieth year, he is given a triumph: an arch of flowers at the end of the avenue and a procession beneath his windows that takes six hours to pass, schoolchildren and workers' delegations and the societies of the city. He stands at the open window with his grandchildren beside him. In June the celebrations resume, and on the twenty-eighth the city takes Eylau off the avenue and puts his name on it instead. Letters begin reaching him addressed to Monsieur Victor Hugo, in his avenue, in Paris.
suggested_refs: The Paris municipal decree of 28 June 1881 renaming the avenue d'Eylau

stops.name: Paris, the death of Juliette Drouet
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the verified sources; the May day is not carried by them
stops.campa: She dies of cancer fifty years after the February night she counted her life from. She has spent them copying his manuscripts in her clear hand, keeping his accounts, following him to Brussels and Jersey and Guernsey and back, and writing to him every day of it; roughly twenty thousand of her letters survive and hardly any of his answers. Her share of the record is almost the whole of it. He is too ill to walk behind the coffin, and she is buried at Saint-Mandé without him. He writes almost nothing after this.
suggested_refs: Juliette Drouet's grave at Saint-Mandé
The published editions of the Drouet correspondence

stops.name: 50 avenue Victor-Hugo, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He takes cold at the beginning of May, it goes to his lungs, and he dies in the afternoon of the twenty-second at eighty-three, in a house on a street with his own name on it. Bulletins have been posted daily and the avenue has been full for a week. The will is written and short: fifty thousand francs to the poor, the hearse of the poor for himself, and no prayer from any church. In a notebook there is a line his executors find and read as a last word, though he may only have been writing a line.
stops.quote_source: Hugo's last notebook, as reported in standard biography (Robb 1997); its status as a final testament is disputed
suggested_refs: Hugo's holograph will, refusing the prayer of all churches

stops.name: Arc de Triomphe, the night of the lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested; the crowd figures in the sources vary and are given as estimates
stops.campa: The body is placed under the Arc de Triomphe on a catafalque draped in black, braziers burning at the corners, cuirassiers standing at it all night while the crowd files past. The theatres are closed. The city has never done this for a writer and has no precedent to work from, so it borrows the forms it uses for generals and heads of state. The coffin under the drapery is the plain one his will specified. The braziers are fed through the night, and the queue is still moving when it gets light.
suggested_refs: Photographs and prints of the catafalque under the Arc de Triomphe, 31 May 1885

stops.name: Panthéon, the crypt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; crowd estimates run to two million and are not independently verifiable
stops.campa: The procession leaves the Arc in the morning and reaches the Panthéon in the afternoon, the route lined the whole way, the estimates running past two million people, more than the city holds. The church has been deconsecrated for the occasion and turned back into a mausoleum. He is laid in the crypt with Voltaire and Rousseau, which is the argument the Republic is making by putting him there. At the head of the column, as instructed, goes the poor man's hearse, under wreaths arriving by the cartload.
suggested_refs: The Panthéon crypt, where Zola joined him in 1908 and Dumas in 2002
Louis Braille was reinterred in the same crypt in 1952
